analysis.one_liner: Rebuilds the legal wall separating insured banks from investment banking and securities trading.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would restore a core piece of the Glass-Steagall Act, the Depression-era law that kept two kinds of finance apart: banks that take federally insured deposits, and firms that underwrite and trade stocks and bonds. It would bar insured banks from being affiliated with brokers, dealers, investment advisers, or investment companies; bar securities-firm executives from serving on bank boards; repeal the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that allowed financial holding companies to combine both businesses; and require existing combinations to unwind within two years, with limited extensions. Its aim is to keep taxpayer-backed deposits from underwriting securities-market risk.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. Insured deposits would no longer sit inside firms that underwrite or trade securities, so savers' federally protected money would be walled off from securities-market losses, and the FDIC's deposit-insurance backstop would apply to a narrower, less speculative banking business [S2][S3]. Traditional deposit-focused banks would also face less competition from conglomerates operating across both businesses [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors and taxpayers backing bank deposits

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits an insured depository institution from being an affiliate of any broker or dealer, investment adviser, investment company, or other securities firm [S2][S3].

Bars officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving on the boards of insured banks, with a narrow agency exception, and requires current dual-serving individuals to end the arrangement within 60 days [S2][S3].

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that let financial holding companies combine banking with securities activities, including financial subsidiaries of national banks, and requires existing affiliations to be wound down within two years, with extensions of up to a year in limited cases [S3].

Restores the Supreme Court's narrow interpretation of the bank-securities wall in Investment Company Institute v. Camp and forbids regulators or courts from reading the new limits more loosely than that decision [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large financial conglomerates. Banks and their holding companies would have to divest securities affiliates, securities firms would lose access to insured-deposit funding and bank distribution, and shareholders of firms like universal banks would absorb the disruption of unwinding. Some customers might lose one-stop financial services [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a hard two-year deadline for unwinding existing bank-securities affiliations, with agency extensions capped at one year, which would force major divestitures and restructuring on a tight clock [S3].

Opponents of restoring Glass-Steagall argue the wall would not by itself prevent banking crises, since pure deposit-taking banks have also failed, and that the riskiest post-1999 activities fall outside this bill's affiliation limits. Supporters respond that the statute caps the federal safety net's reach, not every possible failure mode. This is a good-faith disagreement about how much protection the separation actually buys.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill is straightforward: federally insured deposits are a taxpayer-backed subsidy, and the bill would stop that subsidy from financing securities underwriting and trading. The cost is real but borne narrowly — large conglomerates would restructure, and some consumers might lose combined services. The honest caveat is that separation is a risk-containment measure, not a guarantee against bank failures; it narrows what the government's deposit guarantee covers rather than eliminating financial risk. On balance the protections run to depositors and taxpayers, while the costs run to the largest financial firms — the reverse of how the current arrangement allocates risk.

outcome.mechanism: Sen. Harkin introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on May 16, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5][S3].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial holding companies that combine deposit-taking with securities businesses — they kept their structure intact rather than facing a mandated two-year unwind [S3]. Depositors and taxpayers remain exposed to whatever risk the current combined structure carries. (Short version:) Large universal banks kept their combined structure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large universal banks kept their structure

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Return to Prudent Banking Act of 2013 and sought Senate consideration [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, 113th Congress (chaired by Sen. Tim Johnson of South Dakota)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report — so it never reached the Senate floor [S5].

against.name: Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year session [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no senator beyond the sponsor signed on, so there is no roll-call record of how either party lined up [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Universal banks and financial holding companies
industries.note: These firms would have to divest their securities affiliates within two years, breaking the combined banking-and-trading model allowed since Gramm-Leach-Bliley [S3]. Their interest in keeping the combined model runs against depositors, since the same insured deposits would continue to sit alongside securities operations [S2][S3].
They would lose the ability to affiliate with insured banks and to place executives on bank boards, cutting off access to insured-deposit funding and banking channels [S2][S3].
These banks would face less competition from conglomerates operating across both banking and securities, though some might lose cross-selling services their customers use [S3].
